note: Verifies the NATS 2.14 JetStream message-scheduler protocol: which Nats-Schedule values the server accepts, a CLI-vs-server contract mismatch, rollup replace, source downsampling, and restart durability. These are deterministic accept/reject and render-style observations on nats-server 2.14.2, not a timing distribution. One small timing figure (inter-arrival drift) is included and labeled.
subject: nats-server 2.14.2 (JetStream API Level 4)
method: A message-scheduler stream is created with --allow-schedules. A control message carrying a Nats-Schedule header is published; acceptance is judged by whether the control message persists in the store (nats stream get) versus the server returning an error. See run.sh + fixture/schedule-cases.tsv.

cases.note: 6-field cron WITH seconds — NATS cron is 6-field

cli_server_mismatch.claim: The CLI flag `nats publish --schedule-after=DURATION` (documented by CLI 0.4.0 as 'after a certain duration') is REJECTED by the 2.14.2 server with error 10189 'message schedules pattern is invalid'.
cli_server_mismatch.evidence: 5s and 30s both reproduced 5x, all failing. The CLI surfaces a convenience flag that emits a pattern (@after/@in family) the 2.14.2 server does not implement — a CLI-vs-server contract mismatch.
cli_server_mismatch.workaround: Build the relative one-shot on the caller side as @at <now+duration> and send that.
cli_server_mismatch.trap: Feeding a standard 5-field crontab is silently rejected — the first pitfall for a user expecting 'minute-granularity cron'.

behaviors_verified.claim: Because scheduler control messages carry Nats-Rollup: sub, re-publishing a new schedule to the SAME subject atomically overwrites the previous one.
behaviors_verified.evidence: r.job set to @every 5s, then 1s later re-published as @every 1s: exactly one control message remains (replaced) and the firing cadence switches to 1s (6 firings in 6s). Change/cancel a schedule by re-publishing/deleting on the same subject.

behaviors_verified.claim: Nats-Schedule-Source makes each tick emit only the LATEST value seen on the source subject — a downsampler.
behaviors_verified.evidence: @every 2s + source=src.sensor, then reading-1..30 flooded at 0.3s spacing into src.sensor: target sf.sensor emitted only each 2s tick's latest value: reading-7, 13, 19, 25, 30, 30. Without a source, the control message's own body is re-published every tick.
behaviors_verified.use_case: telemetry / 'last value every N seconds' sampling of a high-frequency source.

behaviors_verified.claim: Schedules survive a server restart; a missed one-shot fires once on recovery; a missed repeating schedule does NOT backfill — it resumes forward only.
behaviors_verified.evidence: @every 2s + a one-shot @at due at :39 during downtime -> server killed 22:06:34 -> ~18s down -> restarted with the same -sd store. Observed: schedules survived (persisted as stream messages); the overdue one-shot fired exactly once on recovery (df.once: 1, not dropped, not duplicated); @every did not replay the ~9 missed ticks (~+5 firings at ~8s after restart, i.e. 2s cadence resumed). No catch-up thundering herd = safe default.

timing_observation.value: 16 firings at @every 1s had inter-arrival exactly 1.000s, drift 0
timing_observation.basis: second-granularity store timestamps; sub-millisecond drift was NOT measured
timing_observation.note: wall-clock aligned; the one quantitative figure in this run.

honest_limits: Single-node verification only. JetStream Raft replication, leader failover, and --replicas>=3 guarantees were NOT verified here. Any 'the scheduler gives you distributed durability' claim is out of this bench's scope.
at-least-once delivery model — firing messages may be duplicated (consumer-side idempotency needed), same as ordinary JetStream.
Accuracy is measured against second-granularity store timestamps; sub-ms drift is not measured. Second-alignment is accurate at 1s/2s/3s cadence.
All results are pinned to nats-server 2.14.2 + nats CLI 0.4.0. A patch release may change CLI flags or accepted syntax.
